Source: https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/BridgeExtensions

# Built-in BridgeExtensions

tentap comes with multiple bridges extensions out of the box, in this page we will show all of them and show their relevant configurations, which can be configured with `BridgeExtension.configureExtension`:

### CoreExtension

uses `@tiptap/extension-document` `@tiptap/extension-paragraph` `@tiptap/extension-text`

This bridge extension includes fundamental logic that is needed to interact with the editor

### BlockquoteBridge

uses `@tiptap/extension-blockquote`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/nodes/blockquote#settings

### CodeBridge

uses `@tiptap/extension-code`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/marks/code#settings

### ItalicBridge

uses `@tiptap/extension-italic`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/marks/italic#settings

### BoldBridge

uses `@tiptap/extension-bold`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/marks/bold#settings

### StrikeBridge

uses `@tiptap/extension-strike`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/marks/strike#settings

### BulletListBridge

uses `BulletList` and `ListItem` from `@tiptap/extension-list`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/nodes/bullet-list#settings

### OrderedListBridge

uses `OrderedList` and `ListItem` from `@tiptap/extension-list`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/nodes/ordered-list#settings

### HeadingBridge

uses `@tiptap/extension-heading`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/nodes/heading#settings

### ListItemBridge

You can use only OrderedListBridge/BulletListBridge for lists, use ListItemBridge in case you want to control lift/sink of lists
uses `ListItem` from `@tiptap/extension-list`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/nodes/list-item#settings

List items always contain a paragraph, so `getHTML()` returns `<li><p>…</p></li>`. See [Rendering editor HTML](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/renderHtml).

### HistoryBridge

uses `UndoRedo` from `@tiptap/extensions` (TipTap v3 renamed the History extension to UndoRedo)
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/extensions/history#settings

Since 1.0 the bridge's name is `undoRedo`. The bridge config is also sent under the old name `history`, so custom editor bundles built against 0.7.x still receive it. If you look a bridge up by name, for example `TenTapStartKit.filter((b) => b.name !== 'history')`, use `'undoRedo'`.

### ColorBridge

uses `@tiptap/extension-color` `@tiptap/extension-text-style`
no relevant configuration

### HighlightBridge

uses `@tiptap/extension-highlight` `@tiptap/extension-text-style`
no relevant configuration

### ImageBridge

uses `@tiptap/extension-image`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/nodes/image#settings

Images are **block** nodes by default, so an `<img>` inside a `<p>` is moved out of the paragraph when content is loaded. To keep images inline:

```tsx
const editor = useEditorBridge({
  bridgeExtensions: [
    ...TenTapStartKit,
    ImageBridge.configureExtension({ inline: true }),
  ],
});
```

Attributes the image schema doesn't know, like `style` or `width`, are dropped when content is parsed. Add them with `ImageBridge.extendExtension` if you need them. When styling images with CSS, scope the rules as `img:not(.ProseMirror-separator)`: ProseMirror adds a hidden separator `<img>` after inline nodes at the end of a line.

### LinkBridge

uses `@tiptap/extension-link`, pre-configured with `{ openOnClick: false, autolink: true }`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/marks/link#settings

When a link is set from the toolbar or with `setLink`, a URL without a scheme gets `https://` added, so `www.google.com` becomes `https://www.google.com` instead of a relative link. A plain email address such as `support@acme.com` becomes a `mailto:` link. URLs that already have a scheme (`http:`, `https:`, `mailto:`, `tel:`, app schemes) and relative or anchor links (`/path`, `#section`, `?query`) are kept as they are. To use another default, configure `defaultProtocol`:

```tsx
LinkBridge.configureExtension({ openOnClick: false, autolink: true, defaultProtocol: 'http' });
```

### TaskListBridge

uses `TaskList` and `TaskItem` from `@tiptap/extension-list`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/nodes/task-list#settings

### UnderlineBridge

uses `@tiptap/extension-underline`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/marks/underline#settings

### PlaceholderBridge

uses `Placeholder` from `@tiptap/extensions`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/extensions/placeholder#settings

### DropCursorBridge

uses `Dropcursor` from `@tiptap/extensions`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/extensions/dropcursor#settings

### HardBreakBridge

uses `@tiptap/extension-hard-break`
relevant configuration: https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/api/nodes/hard-break#settings

## Writing your own bridge

See the [advanced setup](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/setup/advancedSetup) for building a bridge with its own TipTap extension. `extendEditorInstance` receives the same five arguments as in 1.0, plus an optional sixth `context` argument (type `BridgeContext`). It gives your bridge the same message queue the built-in bridges use, so commands sent before the editor is ready aren't lost:

```ts
import { BridgeExtension } from '@10play/tentap-editor';

type MyMessage = { type: string; payload?: unknown };
type MyEditorInstance = {
  myCommand: () => void;
  myQuery: () => Promise<string>;
};

declare module '@10play/tentap-editor' {
  interface EditorBridge extends MyEditorInstance {}
}

export const MyBridge = new BridgeExtension<{}, MyEditorInstance, MyMessage>({
  forceName: 'myBridge',
  extendEditorInstance: (
    sendBridgeMessage,
    _webviewRef,
    _editorState,
    _setEditorState,
    _platform,
    context
  ) => ({
    myCommand: () => sendBridgeMessage({ type: 'my-command' }),
    myQuery: () =>
      context
        ? context.rpc<string>({ type: 'my-query' })
        : Promise.reject(new Error('Needs @10play/tentap-editor 1.1')),
  }),
});
```

`context.rpc` adds a `messageId` to the message payload and resolves with the `content` of the first reply whose `payload.messageId` matches, so the web side of your bridge answers with `sendMessageBack({ type: 'my-query-back', payload: { content, messageId } })`.

`context.supports(capability)` tells you whether the editor bundle in the WebView supports a feature, which is useful when your app may run against a custom bundle built with an older version. The 1.1 web editor advertises `'insertContent'`, `'selectedText'`, `'parseOptions'`, `'styles'`, `'containerHeight'`, `'setDynamicHeight'` and `'inputMode'`; a bundle built with 1.0 or older advertises none. Until the editor is ready, `supports` returns `false`. `rpc` takes an optional second argument: with `{ capability }` it rejects with `TentapUnsupportedError` when the bundle lacks that capability (this is how `getSelectedText` handles older bundles), and `timeoutMs`, which overrides [rpcTimeoutMs](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/useEditorBridge#rpctimeoutms) for that call. The `BridgeContext`, `RpcOptions`, `SendOptions`, `Capabilities` and `CapabilityName` types are exported from `@10play/tentap-editor`.

---

Source: https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/useEditorContent

# useEditorContent

The useEditorContent hook is designed to efficiently retrieve the content. It monitors changes to the editor's content, and reduces unnecessary data exchanges between web and native, optimizing performance and minimizing message traffic.

#### editor

`EditorBridge` (required)

### options

#### type

`EditorContentType`  
default: `'html'`
The type of content to return, `html` and `text` return strings, `json` returns an object.

#### debounceInterval

`number`  
default: `10`

### Usage

```tsx
const content = useEditorContent(editor, { type: 'html' });
useEffect(() => {
  // Will render each time content is updated and call onSave
  content && onSave(content);
}, [content]);
```

Internally `useEditorContent` will get the content by calling `editor.getHTML` (or text/json depending on the `type` option). To reduce
traffic it is called within a `debounce` with a default interval of `10`ms. This can be modified changing the `debounceInterval` option.

The content is fetched once when the editor is ready and then again only when the content changes, not when the selection moves. If responses arrive out of order, an older one never overwrites a newer one, and nothing is fetched after the component unmounts.

In addition we can also get the content as text or as a json.

If you display the HTML outside the editor, for example with `react-native-render-html`, see [Rendering editor HTML](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/renderHtml).

---

Source: https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/CustomKeyboardUtils

# Custom Keyboard Utils

A custom keyboard replaces the system keyboard with a React Native view, such as a color picker or a sticker panel, while the editor stays focused. In this page we will show the APIs of the custom keyboard utils.
For examples please see: [Create custom keyboard](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/customKeyboard) or [Using the ColorKeyboard](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/colorKeyboard)

## How it works

The keyboard is an ordinary view rendered by `CustomKeyboard` in your own React tree, so it has access to your context providers, state and navigation, and it re-renders like any other component. When it opens, the system keyboard is hidden natively while the editor's WebView keeps focus, so the caret, the selection, a hardware keyboard and IME composition all survive switching between the system and the custom keyboard.

Switching is done by a **driver**:

- **Native driver** (default): uses the `TenTapKeyboard` native module that ships with the package. Needs a native rebuild after installing.
- **Fallback driver**: JavaScript only. Used automatically when the native module isn't available (Expo Go, web, a build without the module), when the editor is inside a `Modal` on Android, and when the native driver fails its self-check. It hides the system keyboard with `inputmode="none"` on the editor. See [limitations](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/CustomKeyboardUtils#limitations).

## CustomKeyboard

A react component that renders the active custom keyboard. Render it under your toolbar, as the last child of the same bottom [EditorKeyboardAvoidingView](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/CustomKeyboardUtils#editorkeyboardavoidingview), or with `layout="overlay"` after it (see [Layouts](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/customKeyboard#layouts)). In development on iOS, a warning is logged if the inline keyboard doesn't end at the bottom of the window.

#### keyboards

`CustomKeyboardExtension[]`  
list of [CustomKeyboardExtension's](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/CustomKeyboardUtils#customkeyboardextension)

#### activeKeyboardID

`string | undefined`  
the id of the custom keyboard to show. Changing it from an id to `undefined` closes the custom keyboard and brings the system keyboard back.

#### setActiveKeyboardID

`(id: string | undefined) => void`  
called by `CustomKeyboard` when the keyboard closes on its own (see [closing](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/CustomKeyboardUtils#closing)), so your state stays in sync. Usually the setter of a `useState`.

#### editor

`EditorBridge`  
the editors `EditorBridge` instance

#### rootBackground

`ColorValue`  
default: `editor.theme.colorKeyboard.keyboardRootColor`
The background of the area the custom keyboard is drawn in, on both platforms.

#### layout

`'inline' | 'overlay'`  
default: `'inline'`

- `'inline'`: `CustomKeyboard` takes up the keyboard's height in the layout, so a `KeyboardAvoidingView` around the toolbar and the keyboard keeps the toolbar in place. This is the 0.7.x layout.
- `'overlay'`: `CustomKeyboard` takes no space in the layout and draws the keyboard over the bottom of the screen. Lift your toolbar yourself, with [EditorKeyboardAvoidingView](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/CustomKeyboardUtils#editorkeyboardavoidingview), [useCustomKeyboardHeight](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/CustomKeyboardUtils#usecustomkeyboardheight) or [useKeyboard](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/CustomKeyboardUtils#usekeyboard). Recommended for edge-to-edge apps and for apps using `react-native-keyboard-controller`.

#### defaultHeight

`number`  
default: 38% of the window height
The custom keyboard has the same height as the last system keyboard shown in the current orientation. `defaultHeight` is used before any system keyboard has been shown.

#### closeOnEditorPress

`boolean`  
default: `true`
Close the custom keyboard and bring back the system keyboard when the user taps the editor.

#### androidKeyboardMode

`'system' | 'stable'`  
default: `'system'`
Android only.

- `'system'` never changes your window's `softInputMode`. With `adjustResize` the window resizes when the system keyboard hides, which can shift the toolbar for about a frame during the switch.
- `'stable'` sets `adjustNothing` on the activity window while `CustomKeyboard` is mounted (API 30+, restored on unmount), so the switch has no shift. Other inputs on the same screen are then no longer resized for; use `EditorKeyboardAvoidingView` or `KeyboardAvoidingView` for them. Ignored below API 30 and inside a `Modal`.

Edge-to-edge apps don't need `'stable'`: their window never resizes.

#### forceFallback

`boolean`  
default: `false`
Always use the JavaScript fallback driver, even when the native module is available.

#### onOpen

`(id: string) => void`  
Called when a custom keyboard has finished opening, with its id.

#### onClose

`() => void`  
Called when the custom keyboard has finished closing.

#### onKeyboardError

`(event: KeyboardErrorEvent) => void`

```ts
interface KeyboardErrorEvent {
  reason: 'verify-timeout' | 'native-error';
  driver: 'native' | 'fallback' | 'inline';
  error?: unknown;
}
```

- `'verify-timeout'`: the system keyboard was still up 600 ms after the driver tried to hide it. If the native driver failed, `CustomKeyboard` switches to the fallback driver for as long as it stays mounted. If the fallback failed too, the custom keyboard closes and the system keyboard stays.
- `'native-error'`: the native module threw; `error` holds what it threw.

A warning is also logged in development.

#### onKeyboardHideAndroid

`() => void`  
**Deprecated**, use `onClose`. Kept from 0.7.x. Called on both platforms when the system keyboard comes back while a custom keyboard is up.

#### rootRef

`React.RefObject<any>`  
**Deprecated, ignored.** Needed by the iOS keyboard in 0.7.x. You can remove it.

## CustomKeyboardExtension

A class that defines a custom keyboard.

```tsx
const StickerKeyboard = new CustomKeyboardExtension(
  'keyboard.sticker',
  StickerKeyboardComp,
  { height: 280 } // optional
);
```

#### id

`string`  
a unique key for the custom keyboard

#### comp

`ComponentType`  
The custom keyboard component. It is rendered inside your app like any other component and receives:

| prop | type | description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `editor` | `EditorBridge` | the editor the keyboard belongs to |
| `close` | `() => void` | closes the custom keyboard and brings back the system keyboard |
| `keyboardHeight` | `number` | the height the keyboard is drawn at |

The props type is exported as `CustomKeyboardComponentProps`. Components written for 0.7.x that take no props keep working.

#### options.height

`number`  
optional
A fixed height in dp for this keyboard, instead of following the system keyboard's height.

The constructor still registers the component with `AppRegistry` under `id`, as in 0.7.x. tentap no longer uses that registration.

## ColorKeyboard

A ready-made `CustomKeyboardExtension` (id `keyboard.color`) with text color and highlight buttons. Picking a color applies it and focuses the editor, which returns to the system keyboard. Colors and styles come from the [`colorKeyboard` theme](../examples/customTheme.md#color-keyboard-theme). See the [ColorKeyboard example](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/colorKeyboard).

## useCustomKeyboard

```ts
const { activeKeyboardID, open, close, dismiss } = useCustomKeyboard(); // or useCustomKeyboard(editor)
```

A hook to control the custom keyboard from your own components, such as a toolbar button or the keyboard itself. It can be called anywhere, not only inside `CustomKeyboard`. It controls:

1. the `CustomKeyboard` of `editor`, when you pass one;
2. otherwise, the `CustomKeyboard` rendering the component that calls it (inside a keyboard component);
3. otherwise, the most recently mounted `CustomKeyboard`.

When there is no matching `CustomKeyboard`, `activeKeyboardID` is `undefined` and the functions do nothing.

`open` and `close` go through the same transitions as changing `activeKeyboardID`, and `setActiveKeyboardID` is called so your state follows.

| field | type | description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `activeKeyboardID` | `string \| undefined` | the open custom keyboard |
| `open` | `(id: string) => void` | opens a custom keyboard. Switching from one custom keyboard to another just swaps the content. |
| `close` | `(toSystem?: boolean) => void` | closes the custom keyboard. With `toSystem` (default `true`) the system keyboard comes back; with `false` both are dismissed. |
| `dismiss` | `() => void` | same as `close(false)` |

## useCustomKeyboardHeight

```ts
const height = useCustomKeyboardHeight(); // or useCustomKeyboardHeight(editor)
```

The height of the open custom keyboard, or `0`. Use it with `layout="overlay"` to add space under your toolbar or content, for example when another library already handles the system keyboard. It reads the `CustomKeyboard` of `editor`, or the most recently mounted one.

## EditorKeyboardAvoidingView

A view that adds bottom padding equal to the part of it whichever keyboard covers, system or custom, so the toolbar at its bottom sits fully on top of the keyboard. It measures where it ends in the window and compares that with the top of the keyboard (`useKeyboard().keyboardTop`), so it needs no `keyboardVerticalOffset` below a navigation header or above a tab bar, it covers the navigation bar an edge-to-edge Android keyboard reaches over (also without the native module, as in Expo Go), and it adds nothing where the window already resized for the keyboard (Android `adjustResize` without edge-to-edge). Unlike React Native's `KeyboardAvoidingView` it keeps the same padding while switching between the two keyboards, so the toolbar doesn't move. An inline `CustomKeyboard` inside it takes its own space, so the padding leaves that out.

Place it around the editor and the toolbar (for example inside a `SafeAreaView` with `edges={['top']}`), and put the `Toolbar` in a row so its default `flex: 1` doesn't share the column with the editor:

```tsx
<SafeAreaView style={{ flex: 1 }} edges={['top']}>
  <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={{ flex: 1 }}>
    <View style={{ flex: 1 }}>
      <RichText editor={editor} />
    </View>
    <View style={{ flexDirection: 'row' }}>
      <Toolbar editor={editor} />
    </View>
  </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView>
  <CustomKeyboard layout="overlay" {...keyboardProps} />
</SafeAreaView>
```

Props: all `View` props, plus

| prop | type | default | description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `keyboardVerticalOffset` | `number` | `0` | distance in dp between the bottom of this view and the bottom of the window, subtracted from the padding until the view was measured. Not needed otherwise |
| `enabled` | `boolean` | `true` | `false` removes the padding |

## useKeyboardAccessory

Marks a view that is drawn on top of the keyboard, such as your own toolbar, so that `RichText` keeps the line being typed about one line above it. The library's `Toolbar` does this itself. Pass `false` while the view is hidden.

```tsx
const MyToolbar = ({ editor }: { editor: EditorBridge }) => {
  const { isKeyboardUp } = useKeyboard();
  const accessory = useKeyboardAccessory(isKeyboardUp);
  return <View onLayout={accessory.onLayout}>{/* buttons */}</View>;
};
```

Views that start above the editor (a static toolbar at the top of the screen) are ignored. A toolbar that is not marked still gets the default toolbar height of room when the editor reaches behind the keyboard, but marking it keeps the margin exact.

## useScrollToCaret

A `dynamicHeight` editor is as tall as its content and does not scroll itself, so inside a `ScrollView` the line being typed can grow under the keyboard. `useScrollToCaret` scrolls the `ScrollView` to keep the caret about one line clear of the keyboard, the toolbar on it and the `ScrollView`'s edges:

```tsx
const EditorInScrollView = () => {
  const editor = useEditorBridge({ dynamicHeight: true });
  const scrollViewRef = useRef<ScrollView>(null);
  useScrollToCaret(editor, scrollViewRef);

  return (
    <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={{ flex: 1 }}>
      <ScrollView ref={scrollViewRef} keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled">
        <RichText editor={editor} />
      </ScrollView>
    </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView>
  );
};
```

It needs the web bundle of this version (custom bundles built before 1.1 do not report the caret).

## useKeyboard

```ts
const {
  isKeyboardUp,
  keyboardHeight,
  isCustomKeyboardOpen,
  activeCustomKeyboardID,
  systemKeyboardHeight,
  lastKeyboardHeight,
} = useKeyboard();
```

| field | description |
| --- | --- |
| `isKeyboardUp` | `true` while the system keyboard or a custom keyboard is up |
| `keyboardHeight` | height of whichever keyboard is up. It doesn't drop to `0` while switching between the system and a custom keyboard. |
| `isCustomKeyboardOpen` | `true` while a custom keyboard is open |
| `activeCustomKeyboardID` | id of the open custom keyboard |
| `systemKeyboardHeight` | height of the system keyboard, `0` while it is hidden |
| `lastKeyboardHeight` | the last usable system keyboard height, kept after it hides; `0` before the first one |
| `windowOverlaysKeyboard` | `true` when the keyboard covers the window instead of resizing it: iOS, Android edge-to-edge or `'stable'` mode |
| `keyboardCoverHeight` | how far up from the bottom of the window the keyboard reaches: its height plus, on edge-to-edge Android, the navigation bar it also covers. `0` when no keyboard covers the window, including a system keyboard the window resizes for |
| `inlineKeyboardHeight` | height of the slot an open inline `CustomKeyboard` takes in the layout, `0` for an overlay keyboard or none |
| `keyboardTop` | top of whichever keyboard is up in window coordinates (the space of `measureInWindow`), or `null`. A view whose bottom is `viewBottom` in the window is covered by `Math.max(0, viewBottom - keyboardTop)`. A custom keyboard takes the place of the system keyboard |

Its type is exported as `KeyboardState`.

`isKeyboardUp` and `keyboardHeight` behave as in 1.0 when no custom keyboard is used. Heights are in dp.

## TenTapView

**Deprecated.** The native view used by the 0.7.x keyboard. It now renders nothing and logs a warning in development; remove it from your code.

## Closing

The custom keyboard closes, and `setActiveKeyboardID(undefined)` is called, when:

- the user taps the editor (unless `closeOnEditorPress={false}`): the system keyboard comes back
- you call `editor.focus()`: the system keyboard comes back
- `activeKeyboardID` is set to `undefined`, or `close()` from `useCustomKeyboard` is called
- the editor loses focus, or another input opens the system keyboard
- the Android back button is pressed: both keyboards are dismissed
- the editor's WebView reloads

When `CustomKeyboard` unmounts, the system keyboard suppression is undone, but `setActiveKeyboardID` is not called.

## Types

`CustomKeyboardProps`, `CustomKeyboardComponentProps`, `CustomKeyboardExtensionOptions`, `AnyCustomKeyboardExtension`, `CustomKeyboardControls` (the return type of `useCustomKeyboard`), `EditorKeyboardAvoidingViewProps`, `AndroidKeyboardMode`, `KeyboardErrorEvent`, `KeyboardPhase`, `KeyboardDriverKind`, `KeyboardState` and `TenTapViewProps` are exported from `@10play/tentap-editor`.

## Limitations

- **Android `Modal`:** an editor inside a React Native `Modal` uses the fallback driver, because the modal is a separate window.
- **Fallback driver on iOS:** while a custom keyboard is open, the globe key on a hardware keyboard doesn't work.
- **Fallback driver on Android:** on Android System WebView older than 66, tapping the editor brings back the system keyboard, which closes the custom keyboard.
- **Web:** the custom keyboard renders inline under the toolbar; the browser's keyboard isn't hidden.
- **Floating, split and Stage Manager keyboards** on iPad are not mirrored: the custom keyboard uses the docked keyboard height.

---

Source: https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/basic

# Basic example

In this example we will be creating a basic editor that contains all of the pre-built bridgeExtensions and a toolbar on top of the keyboard. [Jump To Full Example](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/basic#full-example)

## Creating The Editor Bridge

The first thing we want to do is create our [EditorBridge](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/EditorBridge).
To do this we will use the `useEditorBridge` hook. This by default will contain the `TenTapStartKit` which includes all of [the following bridge extensions](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/BridgeExtensions).
Now we have added all of the pre-built bridgeExtensions provided by tentap, and our editor will support all of these bridgeExtensions features

```tsx
const editor = useEditorBridge();
```

This is the same as passing

```tsx
const editor = useEditorBridge({
  bridgeExtensions: TenTapStartKit,
});
```

## Adding the RichText component

Now we will add our RichText component, this is simply a WebView that runs a pre-built tiptap bundle with some extensions, that is then communicated with via our bridgeExtensions

The RichText component receives the EditorBridge we created before

```tsx
<SafeAreaView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}>
  <RichText editor={editor} />
</SafeAreaView>;
```

## Adding a Toolbar on the keyboard

Our RichText is pretty empty without a toolbar, so let's add one.
We wrap the editor and the toolbar in an `EditorKeyboardAvoidingView`, which makes room for the keyboard so the toolbar sits right on top of it:

```tsx
<SafeAreaView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}>
  <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}>
    <View style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}>
      <RichText editor={editor} />
    </View>
    <View style={exampleStyles.toolbarRow}>
      <Toolbar editor={editor} />
    </View>
  </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView>
</SafeAreaView>;
```

`EditorKeyboardAvoidingView` measures how far the keyboard reaches into it, so it needs no `keyboardVerticalOffset` below a navigation header and it also works on edge-to-edge Android. The `Toolbar` shows itself while the editor is focused and the keyboard is up, and the editor keeps the line being typed above it. See [Keyboard and caret](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/setup/keyboard).

> The 1.0 version of this example, with React Native's `KeyboardAvoidingView` absolutely positioned at the bottom of the screen, keeps working. See [the 1.0 layout](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/setup/keyboard#the-10-layout).

## Full Example

```tsx
import React from 'react';
import { StyleSheet, View } from 'react-native';
import { SafeAreaView } from 'react-native-safe-area-context';
import {
  EditorKeyboardAvoidingView,
  RichText,
  Toolbar,
  useEditorBridge,
} from '@10play/tentap-editor';

export const Basic = () => {
  const editor = useEditorBridge({
    autofocus: true,
    avoidIosKeyboard: true,
    initialContent,
  });

  return (
    <SafeAreaView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}>
      <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}>
        <View style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}>
          <RichText editor={editor} />
        </View>
        <View style={exampleStyles.toolbarRow}>
          <Toolbar editor={editor} />
        </View>
      </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView>
    </SafeAreaView>
  );
};

const exampleStyles = StyleSheet.create({
  fullScreen: {
    flex: 1,
  },
  toolbarRow: {
    flexDirection: 'row',
  },
});

const initialContent = `<p>This is a basic example!</p>`;
```

More screens, including custom keyboards, dynamic height and a navigation header, are in the example apps: [`example/`](https://github.com/10play/10tap-editor/tree/main/example) (React Native CLI) and [`example-expo/`](https://github.com/10play/10tap-editor/tree/main/example-expo) (Expo dev client).

---

Source: https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/workingWithContent

# Working with content

This page shows how to read, set and insert content, and how to read the selected text.

## Keeping the content in state

`onChange` tells you that the content changed, without sending the content itself, because sending the whole document from the WebView on every keystroke is expensive. The easiest way to keep the content in state is [useEditorContent](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/useEditorContent):

```tsx
const editor = useEditorBridge({ initialContent });
const content = useEditorContent(editor, { type: 'html' }); // or 'text' | 'json'

useEffect(() => {
  if (content !== undefined) saveDraft(content);
}, [content]);
```

If you prefer `onChange`, fetch the content yourself, ideally debounced:

```tsx
const saveLater = useMemo(
  () => debounce((html: string) => saveDraft(html), 500),
  []
);

const editor = useEditorBridge({
  onChange: async () => {
    saveLater(await editor.getHTML());
  },
});
```

`onChange` is called with the latest version of your callback, so it can use fresh state.

## Setting content

```tsx
editor.setContent('<p>New content</p>');
editor.setContent({ type: 'doc', content: [/* TipTap JSON */] });
```

`setContent` triggers `onChange` and `useEditorContent` like a user edit. Pass `{ emitUpdate: false }` to replace the content silently, for example when loading a saved draft:

```tsx
editor.setContent(savedHtml, { emitUpdate: false });
```

### Keeping whitespace

ProseMirror collapses runs of spaces in HTML. Pass `parseOptions` to keep them, for the whole editor or for one call:

```tsx
const editor = useEditorBridge({
  initialContent: "<a href='hello'>hello</a>  <a href='world'>world</a>",
  parseOptions: { preserveWhitespace: 'full' },
});

editor.setContent(html, { parseOptions: { preserveWhitespace: 'full' } });
```

With `'full'`, newlines and indentation between tags in pretty-printed HTML become content too. Content stored with `getJSON()` keeps its whitespace exactly without parse options.

## Inserting content

[insertContent](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/EditorBridge#insertcontent) inserts HTML, text or TipTap JSON at the cursor, replacing the selection:

```tsx
<Button
  title="Insert signature"
  onPress={() => editor.insertContent('<p><em>Sent from my phone</em></p>')}
/>
```

The content must fit the editor's schema. Unknown tags are dropped or converted, like when pasting.

## Reading the selected text

[getSelectedText](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/EditorBridge#getselectedtext) reads the selection from the live editor:

```tsx
const selected = await editor.getSelectedText();
```

`editorState.selection.from` and `.to` from [useBridgeState](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/BridgeState#usebridgestate) are ProseMirror positions, not offsets into `getText()`. To read the text of a range you stored earlier, pass it to `getSelectedText`:

```tsx
const { selection } = editor.getEditorState();
// later
const text = await editor.getSelectedText(selection);
```

> **Note: Custom editor bundles**
> `parseOptions`, `insertContent` and `getSelectedText` need the 1.1 web editor. With the [advanced setup](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/setup/advancedSetup), rebuild your editor bundle after upgrading. With an older bundle, `getSelectedText` rejects with `TentapUnsupportedError`.

---

Source: https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/customCss

# Custom CSS and Fonts

In this example we will be adding custom css and fonts

## Adding/Overriding CSS

Each bridge, gives us the option to `configureCSS`. Some bridges come with css already configured in them, when we can override by configuring.
Let's give an example by overriding the CodeBridge.

First let's define the css

```ts
const customCodeBlockCSS = `
code {
    background-color: #ffdede;
    border-radius: 0.25em;
    border-color: #e45d5d;
    border-width: 1px;
    border-style: solid;
    box-decoration-break: clone;
    color: #cd4242;
    font-size: 0.9rem;
    padding: 0.25em;
}
`;
```

Now let's configure the CodeBridge to use this css

```tsx
const editor = useEditorBridge({
  bridgeExtensions: [
    // It is important to spread StarterKit BEFORE our extended plugin,
    // as plugin duplicated will be ignored
    ...TenTapStartKit,
    CodeBridge.configureCSS(customCodeBlockCSS), // Custom codeblock css
  ],
});
```

> NOTE calling configureCSS more than once will override the previous css.

## Dynamically Updating CSS

Let's say we want to dynamically update css after the editor is initialized.
We can do this with [injectCSS](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/EditorBridge#injectcss).
`injectCSS` receives two parameters:

- `css`: the css to inject
- `tag`: the tag of the stylesheet of which to inject the css into

When we call `injectCSS` it gets or creates a stylesheet with the given `tag` and updates it's css.

If we wanted to update our `CodeBridge` css after it has been initialized we could run

```ts
editor.injectCSS(ourCustomCSS, CodeBridge.name);
```

then this would replace or create the existing css with whatever we have given it.

Now let's say that we don't want to override a bridges existing css, we could do this by providing a custom tag

```ts
editor.injectCSS(ourCustomCSS, 'our-custom-tag');
```

This will create a new stylesheet with `our-custom-tag` and it will not override any bridge's custom css.

`injectCSS` can be called at any time: calls made before the editor has loaded are queued, and the stylesheet is applied again if the WebView reloads.

## Adding Custom Fonts

There are two ways to load a font into the editor: from a file (recommended), or embedded as base64 in the CSS.

In both cases pass the CSS through `configureCSS` rather than `injectCSS`, so the font is part of the editor from the first paint.

### Loading fonts from a file

Loading the font from a local file avoids sending and parsing a large base64 string every time the editor loads.

1. Get a local file URI for the font. With Expo, use `expo-asset`; in a bare app, copy the font into your app bundle and build the path yourself.
2. Reference it from an `@font-face` rule and pass the CSS to `CoreBridge.configureCSS`.
3. Allow the WebView to read local files. On iOS, also set [webviewBaseURL](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/useEditorBridge#webviewbaseurl) to a `file://` directory that contains the font.
4. Create the editor only once the URI is known, because bridge CSS is read when the editor is created.

```tsx
import { useAssets } from 'expo-asset';

export const EditorWithFont = () => {
  const [assets] = useAssets([require('./assets/Rubik-Regular.ttf')]);
  const fontUri = assets?.[0]?.localUri;
  if (!fontUri) return null;
  return <Editor fontUri={fontUri} />;
};

const Editor = ({ fontUri }: { fontUri: string }) => {
  const editor = useEditorBridge({
    webviewBaseURL: fontUri.substring(0, fontUri.lastIndexOf('/') + 1),
    bridgeExtensions: [
      ...TenTapStartKit,
      CoreBridge.configureCSS(`
        @font-face {
          font-family: 'Rubik';
          src: url('${fontUri}');
        }
        * {
          font-family: 'Rubik', sans-serif;
        }
      `),
    ],
  });

  return (
    <RichText
      editor={editor}
      allowFileAccess
      allowFileAccessFromFileURLs
    />
  );
};
```

### Embedding fonts as base64

This needs no setup, at the cost of a larger editor HTML that is parsed on every load.

So first we need to download and convert our font, so we can inject it into the webview:

1. Upload your font files to https://transfonter.org and check the 'base64' option. When you download the zip file, there will be a `stylesheet.css` file there.
2. Copy the contents of the `stylesheet.css` into a new ts file and export it as a string.

```ts
export const ProtestRiotFont = `
  font-family: 'Protest Riot';
  src: url('data:font/woff2;charset=utf-8;base64,..........
  .......
`;
```

Now we can use our font as follows

```ts
const customFont = `
${ProtestRiotFont}
* {
    font-family: 'Protest Riot', sans-serif;
}
`;
```

And inside our `EditorBridge`

```tsx
const editor = useEditorBridge({
  bridgeExtensions: [
    // It is important to spread StarterKit BEFORE our extended plugin,
    // as plugin duplicated will be ignored
    ...TenTapStartKit,
    CoreBridge.configureCSS(customFont), // Custom font
  ],
});
```

## Chinese, Japanese and Korean text

The default editor doesn't set a font, so the WebView uses its default serif font. For CJK characters it then falls back to a system font that may have no bold or italic variant, and bold or italic text looks unchanged even though the marks are applied. Set a font stack that has CJK weights and let the WebView synthesize the missing styles:

```tsx
const editor = useEditorBridge({
  bridgeExtensions: [
    ...TenTapStartKit,
    CoreBridge.configureCSS(`
      .ProseMirror {
        font-family: -apple-system, system-ui, 'PingFang SC', 'Hiragino Sans GB',
          'Noto Sans CJK SC', 'Microsoft YaHei', sans-serif;
        font-synthesis: weight style;
      }
    `),
  ],
});
```

The default font is unchanged in 1.x so existing editors look the same.

Source: https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/fonts

# Configuring and Extending Extensions

In this example we will configure some extensions. Each bridge comes with the `configureExtension` function, that configures it's underline tiptap extension.
For full list of available configurations for each bridge please see [BridgeExtensions](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/BridgeExtensions).

## Configuring Placeholder and Link

First we can check which options are available to extend on the tiptap docs. Links to them are available [here](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/BridgeExtensions)
In our case let's extend the placeholder to show custom text, and the link extension to not open links when clicking them

```tsx
const editor = useEditorBridge({
  bridgeExtensions: [
    ...TenTapStartKit,
    PlaceholderBridge.configureExtension({
      placeholder: 'Type something...',
    }),
    LinkBridge.configureExtension({ openOnClick: false }),
  ],
});
```

Bridges are deduplicated by name and the last one wins, so spread `TenTapStartKit` first and the configured bridges after it.

## Extending Extension and updating Document Schema

We can also extend the main `tiptapExtension` of each bridge with `extendExtension`.
Let's say we want to update the Document extension of the CoreBridge to mandate a `heading` as the first node:

We could do

```tsx
CoreBridge.extendExtension({ content: 'heading block+' });
```

Now the Document extension will be configured to have a heading node first followed by one or many "blocks"

## Inline Images

Images are block nodes by default, so an `<img>` inside a `<p>` in your `initialContent` is moved out of the paragraph, leaving an empty `<p></p>` behind. To keep images inside paragraphs, configure the ImageBridge:

```tsx
const editor = useEditorBridge({
  bridgeExtensions: [
    ...TenTapStartKit,
    ImageBridge.configureExtension({ inline: true }),
  ],
  initialContent: '<p>Some text <img src="https://example.com/cat.png" /> more text</p>',
});
```

Because extensions are deduplicated by name and the last one wins, the configured ImageBridge replaces the one from `TenTapStartKit`. Attributes like `style` or `width` on `<img>` are dropped unless you add them with `ImageBridge.extendExtension`.

---

Source: https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/navHeader

# Keyboard Avoiding Toolbar with Navigation Header

Below a `react-navigation` header, a `KeyboardAvoidingView` needs a `keyboardVerticalOffset` equal to the header height plus the top inset, and that height changes between platforms and OS versions. A hard-coded value leaves the toolbar partly behind the keyboard.

`EditorKeyboardAvoidingView` does not need the offset. It measures where it ends in the window and pads its bottom by the part of it the keyboard covers, system or custom, including the navigation bar an edge-to-edge Android keyboard also covers, so it works below any header and above a tab bar:

```tsx
import React from 'react';
import { StyleSheet, View } from 'react-native';
import {
  EditorKeyboardAvoidingView,
  RichText,
  Toolbar,
  useEditorBridge,
} from '@10play/tentap-editor';

export const NavigationHeader = () => {
  const editor = useEditorBridge({
    autofocus: true,
    avoidIosKeyboard: true,
  });

  return (
    <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={styles.fullScreen}>
      <View style={styles.fullScreen}>
        <RichText editor={editor} />
      </View>
      <View style={styles.toolbarRow}>
        <Toolbar editor={editor} />
      </View>
    </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView>
  );
};

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  fullScreen: {
    flex: 1,
  },
  // The toolbar's default flex: 1 would share the column with the editor;
  // in a row it only fills the width.
  toolbarRow: {
    flexDirection: 'row',
  },
});
```

The editor keeps the line being typed about a line above the toolbar on its own: `RichText` measures how far the keyboard and the `Toolbar` reach into it, so no `paddingBottom` is needed.

The full screen is in [`example/src/Examples/NavigationHeader.tsx`](https://github.com/10play/10tap-editor/tree/main/example/src/Examples/NavigationHeader.tsx).

If you keep React Native's `KeyboardAvoidingView`, take the offset from the navigator instead of a constant, for example `useHeaderHeight()` from `@react-navigation/elements`.

---

Source: https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/scrollView

# Editor inside a ScrollView

By default the editor fills its container and scrolls its own content. To place it in a form or a screen that scrolls as a whole, let the editor grow with its content and let your `ScrollView` do the scrolling. See [`example-expo/src/screens/DynamicHeight.tsx`](https://github.com/10play/10tap-editor/tree/main/example-expo/src/screens/DynamicHeight.tsx) for a runnable version.

## Dynamic height

With [dynamicHeight](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/useEditorBridge#dynamicheight) the WebView is always as tall as its content. It grows as you type and shrinks when you delete, in a `ScrollView` or in a plain `View`.

```tsx
export const EditorInForm = () => {
  const editor = useEditorBridge({
    dynamicHeight: true,
    initialContent: '<p>Tell us about yourself</p>',
  });
  const scrollViewRef = useRef<ScrollView>(null);
  useScrollToCaret(editor, scrollViewRef);

  return (
    <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={{ flex: 1 }}>
      <ScrollView ref={scrollViewRef} keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled">
        <TextInput placeholder="Title" />
        <RichText editor={editor} />
        <Button title="Save" onPress={save} />
      </ScrollView>
    </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView>
  );
};
```

- Leave `avoidIosKeyboard` off. In dynamic height mode the editor doesn't add keyboard padding, and the parent scroll view doesn't know where the cursor is: the editor is a WebView, not a native text input. Scroll views that follow the focused input, such as `KeyboardAwareScrollView` from `react-native-keyboard-controller`, track native text inputs, so they don't scroll to the cursor inside the editor either.
- [useScrollToCaret](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/CustomKeyboardUtils#usescrolltocaret) does that instead: it scrolls your `ScrollView` so the line being typed stays about one line above the keyboard and the toolbar on it. Without it the cursor of a growing editor ends up under the keyboard.
- `EditorKeyboardAvoidingView` shrinks the scroll view above the keyboard, also on edge-to-edge Android, where the window does not resize. A `KeyboardAvoidingView` with `behavior="padding"` works too.
- Alternatively, [cap the editor's height](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/scrollView#capping-the-height) so that it fits above the keyboard. Once it reaches the cap the editor scrolls itself and keeps the cursor in view.
- `RichText` already passes `scrollEnabled={false}` to the WebView, so only your scroll view scrolls.
- Set `keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled"` on the scroll view, so taps on the toolbar and the link bar reach their buttons while the keyboard is open.

> **Note: react-native-webview version**
> On the new architecture, react-native-webview before 13.13.3 ignores `scrollEnabled={false}`, and WebKit scrolls the WebView to the caret when the keyboard opens. Use 13.13.3 or newer and rebuild your native app. Expo Go ships its own react-native-webview, so test this in a dev build.

## Capping the height

To let the editor grow up to a limit and then scroll internally, cap its container:

```tsx
const editor = useEditorBridge({ dynamicHeight: true });

<RichText editor={editor} containerStyle={{ maxHeight: 300 }} />;
```

Once the cap is reached, the editor keeps its scroll position and the cursor stays in view while you type.

## Reading the content height

The editor reports its content height in px as a `document-height` message. If you need it, for example to animate a container, listen to the messages without turning off tentap's own handling:

```tsx
<RichText
  editor={editor}
  exclusivelyUseCustomOnMessage={false}
  onMessage={(event) => {
    const message = JSON.parse(event.nativeEvent.data);
    if (message.type === 'document-height') setHeight(message.payload);
  }}
/>
```

On Expo web, each editor's `onMessage` only receives that editor's messages, so several editors with `dynamicHeight` can share a page; see [Expo Web Setup](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/setup/expoWeb).

---

Source: https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/renderHtml

# Rendering editor HTML

`getHTML()` and [useEditorContent](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/useEditorContent) return the HTML that TipTap produces. When you display it outside the editor, for example in a read-only list with `react-native-render-html`, a few details of that HTML matter.

## Paragraphs inside list items

In TipTap and ProseMirror a list item always contains a paragraph, so lists come out as:

```html
<ul>
  <li><p>First</p></li>
  <li><p>Second</p></li>
</ul>
```

Web editors hide the paragraph margins with CSS. `react-native-render-html` gives every `<p>` its default vertical margins and doesn't support selectors like `li > p`, so each list item gets extra space. The editor's output can't change without breaking saved content and nested lists, so remove the margins when rendering. A custom `p` renderer can drop them only inside list items:

```tsx
import RenderHtml, { type CustomBlockRenderer } from 'react-native-render-html';

const ParagraphRenderer: CustomBlockRenderer = ({
  TDefaultRenderer,
  tnode,
  style,
  ...props
}) => (
  <TDefaultRenderer
    tnode={tnode}
    {...props}
    style={[
      style,
      tnode.parent?.tagName === 'li' && { marginTop: 0, marginBottom: 0 },
    ]}
  />
);

const renderers = { p: ParagraphRenderer };

<RenderHtml contentWidth={width} source={{ html }} renderers={renderers} />;
```

If you don't need paragraph spacing anywhere, `tagsStyles={{ p: { marginTop: 0, marginBottom: 0 } }}` is enough.

## Task lists

Task lists are `<ul data-type="taskList">` with `<li data-checked="true">` items that contain a `<label>` with a checkbox and a `<div>` with the content. Style or replace them the same way if you render them outside the editor.

## Images

The editor may add a hidden `<img class="ProseMirror-separator">` after an inline node at the end of a line. It is only part of the editor's DOM, not of `getHTML()`, but if you style images with CSS inside the editor, scope the rules as `img:not(.ProseMirror-separator)`.

---

Source: https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/colorKeyboard

# Using The ColorKeyboard

In this example we will add the ColorKeyboard, and a custom button to toggle it in the Toolbar. The same screen is in [`example/src/Examples/Keyboard/WithKeyboard.tsx`](https://github.com/10play/10tap-editor/tree/main/example/src/Examples/Keyboard/WithKeyboard.tsx) and [`example-expo/src/screens/CustomKeyboard.tsx`](https://github.com/10play/10tap-editor/tree/main/example-expo/src/screens/CustomKeyboard.tsx).

## Adding CustomKeyboard Component

First we need a state of the current active keyboard id (used inside the toolbar to show and hide the color keyboard)

```tsx
const [activeKeyboard, setActiveKeyboard] = React.useState<string>();
```

Then, into an `EditorKeyboardAvoidingView` at the bottom of the screen we add the `CustomKeyboard` component, right under the toolbar

```tsx
<EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={exampleStyles.keyboardAvoidingView}>
  <Toolbar editor={editor} />
  <CustomKeyboard
    activeKeyboardID={activeKeyboard}
    setActiveKeyboardID={setActiveKeyboard}
    keyboards={[ColorKeyboard]} // <-- here we add the color keyboard
    editor={editor}
  />
</EditorKeyboardAvoidingView>;
```

## Adding Custom Toolbar

Now that we have added the custom keyboard, we need to add a button to the toolbar so we can open it.
We create a new component `ToolbarWithColor` that adds a button toggling the color keyboard in front of the default items.

```tsx
interface ToolbarWithColorProps {
  editor: EditorBridge;
  activeKeyboard: string | undefined;
  setActiveKeyboard: (id: string | undefined) => void;
}
const ToolbarWithColor = ({
  editor,
  activeKeyboard,
  setActiveKeyboard,
}: ToolbarWithColorProps) => {
  return (
    <Toolbar
      editor={editor}
      items={[
        {
          onPress: () => () => {
            const isActive = activeKeyboard === ColorKeyboard.id;
            if (isActive) editor.focus();
            setActiveKeyboard(isActive ? undefined : ColorKeyboard.id);
          },
          active: () => activeKeyboard === ColorKeyboard.id,
          disabled: () => false,
          image: () => Images.palette,
        },
        ...DEFAULT_TOOLBAR_ITEMS,
      ]}
    />
  );
};
```

The toolbar stays visible while the color keyboard is open. Picking a color applies it and brings the system keyboard back, and tapping the editor closes the color keyboard too.

Then all that is left to replace `Toolbar` with our new `ToolbarWithColor` and we're done!

```tsx
<ToolbarWithColor
  editor={editor}
  activeKeyboard={activeKeyboard}
  setActiveKeyboard={setActiveKeyboard}
/>
```

## Full Example

```tsx
import React from 'react';
import { StyleSheet, View } from 'react-native';
import { SafeAreaView } from 'react-native-safe-area-context';
import {
  ColorKeyboard,
  CustomKeyboard,
  DEFAULT_TOOLBAR_ITEMS,
  EditorKeyboardAvoidingView,
  Images,
  RichText,
  Toolbar,
  useEditorBridge,
  type EditorBridge,
} from '@10play/tentap-editor';

export const WithColorKeyboard = () => {
  const editor = useEditorBridge({
    autofocus: true,
    avoidIosKeyboard: true,
    initialContent: '<p>Select some text and pick a color</p>',
  });
  const [activeKeyboard, setActiveKeyboard] = React.useState<string>();

  return (
    <SafeAreaView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen} edges={['top']}>
      <View style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}>
        <RichText editor={editor} />
      </View>
      <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={exampleStyles.keyboardAvoidingView}>
        <ToolbarWithColor
          editor={editor}
          activeKeyboard={activeKeyboard}
          setActiveKeyboard={setActiveKeyboard}
        />
        <CustomKeyboard
          activeKeyboardID={activeKeyboard}
          setActiveKeyboardID={setActiveKeyboard}
          keyboards={[ColorKeyboard]}
          editor={editor}
        />
      </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView>
    </SafeAreaView>
  );
};

interface ToolbarWithColorProps {
  editor: EditorBridge;
  activeKeyboard: string | undefined;
  setActiveKeyboard: (id: string | undefined) => void;
}

const ToolbarWithColor = ({
  editor,
  activeKeyboard,
  setActiveKeyboard,
}: ToolbarWithColorProps) => {
  return (
    <Toolbar
      editor={editor}
      items={[
        {
          onPress: () => () => {
            const isActive = activeKeyboard === ColorKeyboard.id;
            if (isActive) editor.focus();
            setActiveKeyboard(isActive ? undefined : ColorKeyboard.id);
          },
          active: () => activeKeyboard === ColorKeyboard.id,
          disabled: () => false,
          image: () => Images.palette,
        },
        ...DEFAULT_TOOLBAR_ITEMS,
      ]}
    />
  );
};

const exampleStyles = StyleSheet.create({
  fullScreen: {
    flex: 1,
  },
  keyboardAvoidingView: {
    position: 'absolute',
    width: '100%',
    bottom: 0,
  },
});
```

## Customizing the colors

The colors, their labels and the keyboard's styles come from the `colorKeyboard` key of the editor theme. See [Color keyboard theme](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/customTheme#color-keyboard-theme).

---

Source: https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/customKeyboard

# Custom Keyboard

In this example we will create and add a custom sticker keyboard 👯‍♀️
We go through the code in small chunks; the [full solution](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/customKeyboard#full-solution) is at the end. For the API reference see [Custom Keyboard Utils](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/CustomKeyboardUtils). Runnable versions are in [`example/src/Examples/Keyboard`](https://github.com/10play/10tap-editor/tree/main/example/src/Examples/Keyboard) and [`example-expo/src/screens`](https://github.com/10play/10tap-editor/tree/main/example-expo/src/screens) (inline and overlay layouts).

### First, let's create a new CustomKeyboard

```tsx
const StickerKeyboardComp = ({ editor }: CustomKeyboardComponentProps) => {
  return (
    <View style={keyboardStyles.keyboardContainer}>
      <StickerRow stickers={stickersTop} editor={editor} />
      <StickerRow stickers={stickersBottom} editor={editor} />
    </View>
  );
};

export const StickerKeyboard = new CustomKeyboardExtension(
  'keyboard.sticker',
  StickerKeyboardComp
);
```

- `StickerKeyboardComp` is the view that is shown in place of the system keyboard. It is rendered in your app's own React tree, so it can use your context providers and state, and it re-renders like any other component.
- The keyboard component receives `editor`, `close` and `keyboardHeight` props, typed as `CustomKeyboardComponentProps`. Each sticker calls `editor.setImage(sticker)`.
- `CustomKeyboardExtension` gives the keyboard the id `keyboard.sticker`.

### Now we can use our custom keyboard

```tsx
export const CustomKeyboardExample = () => {
  const editor = useEditorBridge({
    avoidIosKeyboard: true,
    autofocus: true,
    bridgeExtensions: [
      ...TenTapStartKit,
      ImageBridge.configureExtension({ inline: true }),
    ],
  });
  const [activeKeyboard, setActiveKeyboard] = React.useState<string>();

  return (
    <SafeAreaView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen} edges={['top']}>
      <View style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}>
        <RichText editor={editor} />
      </View>
      <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={exampleStyles.keyboardAvoidingView}>
        <StickerToolbar
          activeKeyboard={activeKeyboard}
          setActiveKeyboard={setActiveKeyboard}
          editor={editor}
        />
        <CustomKeyboard
          activeKeyboardID={activeKeyboard}
          setActiveKeyboardID={setActiveKeyboard}
          keyboards={[StickerKeyboard]} // <-- Add our custom keyboard to the keyboards prop
          editor={editor}
        />
      </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView>
    </SafeAreaView>
  );
};
```

- A react state controls which custom keyboard is shown. `CustomKeyboard` calls `setActiveKeyboard(undefined)` itself when the keyboard closes, for example when the user taps the editor.
- `CustomKeyboard` goes right under the toolbar, as the last child of the same `EditorKeyboardAvoidingView`, so the toolbar stays where it is when the keyboards switch. `EditorKeyboardAvoidingView` pads for the system keyboard and leaves out the space the open `CustomKeyboard` takes itself. It also works on edge-to-edge Android (the default in Expo), where the window does not resize for the keyboard, so a React Native `KeyboardAvoidingView` with `behavior="height"` or no behavior, as in 0.7.x, leaves the toolbar behind the keyboard.

### Add button that will toggle our custom keyboard

```tsx
const StickerToolbar = ({
  editor,
  activeKeyboard,
  setActiveKeyboard,
}: ToolbarWithStickersProps) => {
  return (
    <Toolbar
      editor={editor}
      items={[
        {
          onPress: () => () => {
            const isActive = activeKeyboard === StickerKeyboard.id;
            if (isActive) editor.focus();
            setActiveKeyboard(isActive ? undefined : StickerKeyboard.id);
          },
          active: () => activeKeyboard === StickerKeyboard.id,
          disabled: () => false,
          image: () => Images.palette,
        },
        ...DEFAULT_TOOLBAR_ITEMS,
      ]}
    />
  );
};
```

- The [Toolbar](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/Components#toolbar) stays visible while a custom keyboard is open, so no extra `hidden` logic is needed.
- Pressing the button again calls `editor.focus()`, which brings the system keyboard back.

> **Note: Upgrading from 0.7.x**
> The 0.7.x version of this example still works: `rootRef` is ignored, and a toolbar that computes `hidden` from `useKeyboard()` and `activeKeyboard` keeps working. You can remove both.

### Full solution

```tsx
import React from 'react';
import {
  View,
  StyleSheet,
  TouchableOpacity,
  Image,
} from 'react-native';
import { SafeAreaView } from 'react-native-safe-area-context';
import {
  RichText,
  Toolbar,
  useEditorBridge,
  type EditorBridge,
  TenTapStartKit,
  ImageBridge,
  CustomKeyboard,
  CustomKeyboardExtension,
  EditorKeyboardAvoidingView,
  DEFAULT_TOOLBAR_ITEMS,
  Images,
  type CustomKeyboardComponentProps,
} from '@10play/tentap-editor';

const stickersTop = [
  'https://res.cloudinary.com/dkofpy6k6/image/upload/c_fill,g_auto,h_100,w_100/v1707657614/7c1d68c9-126c-4967-a6a4-7252e998802d.png',
  'https://res.cloudinary.com/dkofpy6k6/image/upload/c_fill,g_auto,h_100,w_100/v1707657441/skel_uv9mo1.png',
  'https://res.cloudinary.com/dkofpy6k6/image/upload/c_fill,g_auto,h_100,w_100/v1707657821/ecee86ed-6291-412c-9570-2b561314d723.png',
];
const stickersBottom = [
  'https://res.cloudinary.com/dkofpy6k6/image/upload/c_fill,g_auto,h_100,w_100/v1707658182/53b06114-544c-4048-869f-fedbc6d51bb9.png',
  'https://res.cloudinary.com/dkofpy6k6/image/upload/c_fill,g_auto,h_100,w_100/v1707658198/75fe11eb-1d93-45e4-bb97-d8e26dbe4335.png',
  'https://res.cloudinary.com/dkofpy6k6/image/upload/c_fill,g_auto,h_100,w_100/v1707658214/c6cadcf3-785c-49ec-b34d-c6d8ea544153.png',
];

const StickerRow = ({
  stickers,
  editor,
}: {
  stickers: string[];
  editor: EditorBridge;
}) => {
  return (
    <View style={keyboardStyles.row}>
      {stickers.map((sticker) => (
        <TouchableOpacity
          key={sticker}
          style={keyboardStyles.sticker}
          onPress={() => editor.setImage(sticker)}
        >
          <Image source={{ uri: sticker }} style={keyboardStyles.image} />
        </TouchableOpacity>
      ))}
    </View>
  );
};

const StickerKeyboardComp = ({ editor }: CustomKeyboardComponentProps) => {
  return (
    <View style={keyboardStyles.keyboardContainer}>
      <StickerRow stickers={stickersTop} editor={editor} />
      <StickerRow stickers={stickersBottom} editor={editor} />
    </View>
  );
};

export const StickerKeyboard = new CustomKeyboardExtension(
  'keyboard.sticker',
  StickerKeyboardComp
);

export const CustomKeyboardExample = () => {
  const editor = useEditorBridge({
    avoidIosKeyboard: true,
    autofocus: true,
    bridgeExtensions: [
      ...TenTapStartKit,
      ImageBridge.configureExtension({ inline: true }),
    ],
  });
  const [activeKeyboard, setActiveKeyboard] = React.useState<string>();

  return (
    <SafeAreaView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen} edges={['top']}>
      <View style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}>
        <RichText editor={editor} />
      </View>
      <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={exampleStyles.keyboardAvoidingView}>
        <StickerToolbar
          activeKeyboard={activeKeyboard}
          setActiveKeyboard={setActiveKeyboard}
          editor={editor}
        />
        <CustomKeyboard
          activeKeyboardID={activeKeyboard}
          setActiveKeyboardID={setActiveKeyboard}
          keyboards={[StickerKeyboard]}
          editor={editor}
        />
      </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView>
    </SafeAreaView>
  );
};

interface ToolbarWithStickersProps {
  editor: EditorBridge;
  activeKeyboard: string | undefined;
  setActiveKeyboard: (id: string | undefined) => void;
}

const StickerToolbar = ({
  editor,
  activeKeyboard,
  setActiveKeyboard,
}: ToolbarWithStickersProps) => {
  return (
    <Toolbar
      editor={editor}
      items={[
        {
          onPress: () => () => {
            const isActive = activeKeyboard === StickerKeyboard.id;
            if (isActive) editor.focus();
            setActiveKeyboard(isActive ? undefined : StickerKeyboard.id);
          },
          active: () => activeKeyboard === StickerKeyboard.id,
          disabled: () => false,
          image: () => Images.palette,
        },
        ...DEFAULT_TOOLBAR_ITEMS,
      ]}
    />
  );
};

const keyboardStyles = StyleSheet.create({
  keyboardContainer: {
    alignItems: 'center',
    justifyContent: 'center',
    flex: 1,
    width: '100%',
  },
  row: {
    flex: 1,
    flexDirection: 'row',
    justifyContent: 'center',
    alignItems: 'center',
  },
  sticker: { flex: 1, alignItems: 'center', justifyContent: 'center' },
  image: { width: 100, height: 100 },
});

const exampleStyles = StyleSheet.create({
  fullScreen: {
    flex: 1,
  },
  keyboardAvoidingView: {
    position: 'absolute',
    width: '100%',
    bottom: 0,
  },
});
```

## Layouts

### Inline (default)

The layout above: `CustomKeyboard` takes up the keyboard's height under the toolbar, and an `EditorKeyboardAvoidingView` around both keeps the toolbar in place for the system keyboard. This is the 0.7.x layout with `EditorKeyboardAvoidingView` in place of React Native's `KeyboardAvoidingView`; the 0.7.x version keeps working where the window resizes for the keyboard.

### Overlay with EditorKeyboardAvoidingView

`EditorKeyboardAvoidingView` pads its content by the height of whichever keyboard is up and keeps the same padding while switching, so it doesn't depend on the timing of React Native's keyboard events. Combine it with `layout="overlay"`, and render `CustomKeyboard` after it, outside the padded view:

```tsx
<SafeAreaView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen} edges={['top']}>
  <EditorKeyboardAvoidingView style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}>
    <View style={exampleStyles.fullScreen}>
      <RichText editor={editor} />
    </View>
    {/* In a row, the toolbar's default flex: 1 only fills the width */}
    <View style={{ flexDirection: 'row' }}>
      <StickerToolbar
        activeKeyboard={activeKeyboard}
        setActiveKeyboard={setActiveKeyboard}
        editor={editor}
      />
    </View>
  </EditorKeyboardAvoidingView>
  <CustomKeyboard
    layout="overlay"
    activeKeyboardID={activeKeyboard}
    setActiveKeyboardID={setActiveKeyboard}
    keyboards={[StickerKeyboard]}
    editor={editor}
  />
</SafeAreaView>
```

Here the toolbar is part of the layout instead of being absolutely positioned, and the editor shrinks to make room for whichever keyboard is up.

This is the recommended layout for edge-to-edge Android apps.

### With react-native-keyboard-controller

`react-native-keyboard-controller` only knows about the system keyboard, so its `KeyboardAvoidingView` and `KeyboardStickyView` drop to the bottom while a custom keyboard is open. Use `layout="overlay"` and add the custom keyboard's height yourself with `useCustomKeyboardHeight`:

```tsx
import { KeyboardStickyView } from 'react-native-keyboard-controller';
import { useCustomKeyboardHeight } from '@10play/tentap-editor';

const ToolbarArea = ({
  editor,
  activeKeyboard,
  setActiveKeyboard,
}: ToolbarWithStickersProps) => {
  const customKeyboardHeight = useCustomKeyboardHeight();

  return (
    <KeyboardStickyView
      style={{ position: 'absolute', width: '100%', bottom: 0 }}
      offset={{ closed: -customKeyboardHeight }}
    >
      <StickerToolbar
        editor={editor}
        activeKeyboard={activeKeyboard}
        setActiveKeyboard={setActiveKeyboard}
      />
    </KeyboardStickyView>
  );
};

// somewhere below, outside the sticky view:
<CustomKeyboard
  layout="overlay"
  activeKeyboardID={activeKeyboard}
  setActiveKeyboardID={setActiveKeyboard}
  keyboards={[StickerKeyboard]}
  editor={editor}
/>;
```

## Android: keeping the toolbar still

With the default `androidKeyboardMode="system"` the window keeps your `softInputMode`. With `adjustResize` (the React Native default) the window resizes when the system keyboard hides, and the custom keyboard takes its space only once React Native reports the hide. The toolbar drops to the bottom and comes back up while switching to the custom keyboard, and is pushed up briefly while switching back. To avoid it:

- use the [overlay layout](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/customKeyboard#overlay-with-editorkeyboardavoidingview), or
- set `androidKeyboardMode="stable"` on `CustomKeyboard`. It switches the window to `adjustNothing` while `CustomKeyboard` is mounted (Android 11+), and restores your mode on unmount. It needs the native module, so it has no effect in Expo Go, with the fallback driver or inside a `Modal`. Other inputs on that screen then need a `KeyboardAvoidingView` or `EditorKeyboardAvoidingView`.

Edge-to-edge apps (the default with `targetSdk` 36) are not affected: their window never resizes.

## Expo Go and the fallback driver

Expo Go can't load the native `TenTapKeyboard` module, so `CustomKeyboard` uses the JavaScript fallback driver automatically. No code changes are needed; build a dev client for the native driver. You can also force the fallback with `forceFallback` to compare the two.

The fallback is also used inside a React Native `Modal` on Android, and when the native driver fails its self-check (reported through `onKeyboardError`). See the [limitations](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/CustomKeyboardUtils#limitations).

Source: https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/mentions

# DarkMode

In this example we will implement darkmode in the editor. This is similar to setting up [custom css](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/customCss).

Dark mode has two parts:

- the native side (toolbar, link bar, [color keyboard](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/colorKeyboard), WebView background), styled by the `theme` option;
- the web side (the document inside the WebView), styled with CSS.

## Adding Dark Theme

To use the built-in dark theme on the native side, pass `darkEditorTheme`:

```tsx
const editor = useEditorBridge({
  theme: darkEditorTheme,
});
```

`darkEditorTheme` includes a dark toolbar and a dark `colorKeyboard` theme (`darkColorKeyboardTheme`), so the ColorKeyboard follows too.

Now we just need to update the web-side css with `configureCSS`:

```tsx
import {
  CoreBridge,
  darkEditorCss,
  darkEditorTheme,
  TenTapStartKit,
  useEditorBridge,
} from '@10play/tentap-editor';

const editor = useEditorBridge({
  bridgeExtensions: [
    ...TenTapStartKit,
    CoreBridge.configureCSS(darkEditorCss), // <--- Add our dark mode css
  ],
  theme: darkEditorTheme, // <-- Add our dark mode theme
});
```

## Following the system appearance

`theme` is read on every render, so it can follow `useColorScheme()`. Bridges, and the CSS configured on them, are read once when the editor is created. To switch the web-side CSS at runtime, inject it with [injectCSS](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/api/EditorBridge#injectcss) under its own tag:

```tsx
import React, { useEffect } from 'react';
import { useColorScheme } from 'react-native';
import {
  darkEditorCss,
  darkEditorTheme,
  defaultEditorTheme,
  RichText,
  useEditorBridge,
} from '@10play/tentap-editor';

export const ThemedEditor = () => {
  const dark = useColorScheme() === 'dark';
  const editor = useEditorBridge({
    theme: dark ? darkEditorTheme : defaultEditorTheme,
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    // An empty string clears the stylesheet with this tag.
    editor.injectCSS(dark ? darkEditorCss : '', 'dark-mode');
  }, [dark, editor]);

  return <RichText editor={editor} />;
};
```

`injectCSS` calls made before the editor has loaded are queued, and the stylesheet is applied again if the WebView reloads. Alternatively, remount the screen with a `key` when the scheme changes and pick the bridges for that scheme, as the [`example-expo`](https://github.com/10play/10tap-editor/tree/main/example-expo) app does.

## Customizing

To change the colors, pass a partial theme; it is deep-merged into the default theme. See [Custom Theme](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/customTheme), including the [color keyboard theme](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/customTheme#color-keyboard-theme).

---

Source: https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/customTheme

# Custom Theme

In this example we will add a custom theme

## Adding Custom Theme

We can also provide a custom theme

```tsx
useEditorBridge({
  theme: {
    toolbar: {
      toolbarBody: {
        borderTopColor: '#C6C6C6B3',
        borderBottomColor: '#C6C6C6B3',
        backgroundColor: '#474747',
      },
      // Check the ToolbarTheme type for all options
    },
    webview: {
      backgroundColor: '#1C1C1E',
    },
    webviewContainer: {},
  },
});
```

The theme you pass is deep-merged into the default theme, so you only need to set the keys you change.

## Link bar

The link bar that opens from the toolbar's link button is styled by `toolbar.linkBarTheme`. Its `hintText` key sets the placeholder of the URL input:

```tsx
useEditorBridge({
  theme: {
    toolbar: {
      linkBarTheme: {
        hintText: 'Paste a link',
        placeholderTextColor: '#8E8E93',
      },
    },
  },
});
```

## Color keyboard theme

The [ColorKeyboard](https://10play.github.io/10tap-editor/docs/examples/colorKeyboard) is styled by the `colorKeyboard` key:

```tsx
useEditorBridge({
  theme: {
    colorKeyboard: {
      keyboardRootColor: 'white', // background of the keyboard area
      colorSelection: [
        // Custom colors in color keyboard
        {
          name: 'Custom Color',
          value: '#E5112B',
          displayColor: '#E5112B', // Optional - the color that will be displayed on ui (if left empty will default to use value)
        },
      ],
      // Check the ColorKeyboardTheme type for all options
    },
  },
});
```

`colorSelection` and `highlightSelection` **replace** the default lists instead of being merged with them, so the example above shows a single color. `colorKeyboard` is optional on `EditorTheme`; when it's missing, the default color keyboard theme is used. `darkEditorTheme` includes a dark color keyboard theme.

The `Color` and `ColorKeyboardTheme` types, and the built-in `defaultColorKeyboardTheme` and `darkColorKeyboardTheme`, are exported from `@10play/tentap-editor`, so you can build on the default lists:

```tsx
import { defaultColorKeyboardTheme } from '@10play/tentap-editor';

useEditorBridge({
  theme: {
    colorKeyboard: {
      colorSelection: [
        ...defaultColorKeyboardTheme.colorSelection,
        { name: 'Brand', value: '#E5112B' },
      ],
    },
  },
});
```
